From the Editor's Desk BY JODY DUNCAN We on the Cinefex editorial staff were about a month into our two-month research and writing period for Issue 171 when, in a single day in midMarch, four of the five films we were covering had their release dates pulled due to pandemicrelated movie theater closures. We dubbed it the 'Saint Patrick's Day Massacre,' and it left us shellshocked. Worse, it left us with no new films to cover, and precious little time to come up with new content. It's true, our dilemma paled in comparison to what had befallen those ill with the virus or losing loved ones. To paraphrase a great silverscreen philosopher, the problems of three little visual effects journalists amounted to a hill of beans in this crazy world. But we had to come up with something for our next issue, and we had to do it fast. What was most important, we determined immediately, was to get ourselves back on solid ground, and off the quicksand of constantly shifting film release dates. What could we count on? What entertainment content was going to be there, no matter how bad the pandemic got, or how long the shelter-in-place orders remained in effect? The answer was obvious: content from streaming channels would still air as planned, no matter what, and likely to an even larger audience. We had briefly talked about doing an all-streaming issue in the past. If ever there was a time to do one, it was now. So, here it is, with coverage of six of the most compelling and popular shows available for your viewing pleasure during the Great Stay at Home of spring 2020: Westworld (HBO), Deus (Hulu), Star Trek: Picard (CBS All Access), Tales from the Loop and The Boys (Amazon Prime), and Altered Carbon (Netflix). Sit back, relax, and read the pages of Cinefex 171 to learn all about these fascinating productions. What else have you got to do? We offer our best wishes for good health, sincere sympathies for those suffering from this pandemic, and support to all our friends in the visual effects industry working from home.

After seven seasons and 178 episodes of CBS Television's Star Trek: The Next Generation, and four Paramount Pictures feature films culminating with Star Trek: Nemesis, Picard retired to Earth. The erudite Admiral's spacefaring adventures resulted in many personal sacrifices including the loss of his android friend, Lieutenant Commander Data (Brent Spiner), which haunts Picard in the opening of CBS All Access' Star Trek: Picard. The series was the ninth based on Gene Roddenberry's characters, the second for CBS All Access, and marked a return to Los Angeles-based production, following the Toronto production of the streaming network's inaugural Star Trek: Discovery. A veteran of Discovery, visual effects supervisor Jason Zimmerman stepped up as one of Picard's four supervising producers. "I had an increasing role on both Discovery and Picard," said Zimmerman. Resetting the Wonder BY GRAHAM EDWARDS n an unremarkable meadow near some woods, a small child operates a giant robot by remote control. A boy and an old man investigate a mysterious spherical object abandoned on a barren sandy heath. A trio of enigmatic towers dominates the skyline above an ordinary town. Such are the images conjured by artist Simon Stalenhag in his book Tales from the Loop. First published in 2014, the volume contains paintings combining Stålenhag's twin passions: the landscape of his native Sweden and the futuristic visions of artists like Ralph McQuarrie and Syd Mead. To accompany the paintings, Stalenhag wrote short stories about a secret underground research facility that causes the landscape to fill up with pieces of strange discarded technology - the 'Loop' of the title. Some years after the book's publication, Stålenhag's work came to the attention of 6th & Idaho Productions, the production company owned by filmmaker Matt Reeves. A deal followed with Fox 21 Television Studios to acquire the rights and develop the concept with Amazon Studios for streaming release through Amazon Prime Video. The role 1 / 23 of showrunner went to writer Nathaniel Halpern, known for his work on television shows

THE LOOPI including Outcast and FX Network's Legion. Halpern wrote all eight episodes of Tales from the Loop, drawing inspiration directly from Stålenhag's paintings rather than from the book's written narrative. Like most people, I was taken by Simon's aesthetic," said Halpern, "which is this unique marriage of the ordinary and the extraordinary. More than that, I found the paintings to be quite poignant. I was fascinated by the mixture of emotion and science fiction." Stålenhag's compositions usually place a single futuristic element into an otherwise ordinary setting, and halpern was determined to preserve this distinctive visual language. "For each new painting you look at," Halpern observed, "the sense of wonder is reset. The problem with a television show is the more familiar you get with it, the more you'll take for granted those genre elements. So I decided every story would introduce a different science fiction conceit. That resets the wonder every episode. Halpern structured Tales from the Loop as eight self-contained stories revolving around concepts including time travel, parallel worlds and personality transference. Despite the show's anthological feel, continuing characters and interlinked narratives help weave the disparate storylines into a cohesive whole. Although character and storytelling take center stage, the show relies on a combination of physical set pieces and digital effects to bring Stålenhag's surreal visions to life. Legacy Effects created several practical robots, working in close liaison with the visual effects team, which ultimately delivered around 1,300 visual effects shots. Andrea Knoll took up the role of overall visual effects producer during preproduction. "I had a meeting 2 / 23 with the production designer, Philip Messina, to strategize our approach to key assetsi

Knoll recalled, "which we would mostly be setting up in the pilot. In reading the scripts and doing breakdowns, I had automatically assumed most assets would be full CG. But Philip planned to do a lot practically, which is what we did. And it looked incredible.i Ashley Bernes from Moving Picture Company (MPC) was overall visual effects supervisor on the pilot. Rodeo FX's Robert Bock took over for all the remaining episodes except Episode 6; this was supervised by Eduardo Anton, who also led a small in-house team for the whole season. Rodeo FX was lead vendor throughout. MPC and Bot VFX undertook tasks such as bluescreen composites, cleanup and environment enhancement across three episodes each. ready started post on Episode 1 and we were prepping Episode 3. This continued until filming wrapped, at which point we could focus exclusively on postproduction for the final episodes. Our main objective all the way through was to stay true to Simon's work - not just the look, but also the feel. We wanted every image you see on screen to feel like a painting." Also known as the Loop, its purpose is to unlock and explore the mysteries of the universe. As Loop founder Russ Willard (Jonathan Pryce) remarks, the facility also generates THE LOOP s is common in television, there were typically three episodes underway at any one time. The precise look of the disintegration effect was the subject of much debate.iI worked with a concept artist in preproduction," Ashley Bernes recounted, "and discussed ideas with Nathaniel and Mark Romanek, who directed the pilot. Is it an explosion? Does it shatter? Does it vaporize? Does it get morphed or teleported? We quickly established that the destruction should look as real as possible, it's just that gravity is pointing in the opposite direction. The team studied video of houses collapsing in earthquakes, landslides, sinkholes and other disasters. We made a sizzle reel and rotated it 180 degrees so things were flying upwards. "We had a layer of tech animation on top and we added small details in Nuke, using deep compositing to put extra layers in between the CG renders. We animated things like cables in Nuke, which gave us way more control than doing it in CG." The Data of All Things BY JOE FORDHAM like the strange attraction of particles, some filmmakers naturally gravitate toward a repertory company of collaborators - a trusted cinematographer, a production designer with chameleon-like adaptabilities, the unique ear of a gifted composer, or an alter ego performer. At a pragmatic level, the alliances improve production efficiency and, at best, lead to a unique cross-pollination of ideas. After the one-two punch of the Oscar-winning artificial intelligence thriller Ex Machina and the extraterrestrial mystery Annihilation, filmmaker Alex Garland had accumulated a core creative brain trust. "It's not just me," said visual effects supervisor Andrew Whitehurst. ¿Alex likes to work with a team of people he enjoys and trusts. That includes his producers, production designer Mark Digby, cinematographer Rob Hardy. There are working relationships he's developed over quite a few years now." Garland and Whitehurst's common interests in science led to heady conceptual banter. "I have an interest in multiverse theory, and I was fascinated by the work of physicist David Deutsch, who wrote an amazing book called The Fabric of Reality. DEVS and I talked through those ideas, and our understanding of the science and philosophyi Conversations sparked ideas for a science fiction story, Deus. Andrew and I shared information and theories about science and physics," related Alex Garland. "And we had a rolling conversation, through Ex Machina and Annihilation, about quantum mechanics - how those theories represent the underlying building blocks of everything. I was interested in what quantum computers were able to do, the weird implications of quantum mechanics, and a way of looking at physics that makes the universe deterministic. And I was interested in the capabilities of big, powerful tech companies. That mutated into Deus." Garland's narrative took shape as a high-tech thriller, told over approximately 400 minutes as an eight-part mini-series for FX Network and Hulu. The story revolves around Amaya, a quantum computing campus outside San Francisco run by an introverted technology developer known to all as simply Forest (Nick Offerman). Amaya computer engineer Lily Chan (Sonoya Mizuno) becomes suspicious of Forest's activities after her boyfriend, Sergei (Karl Glusman), joins the secret Devs division and vanishes. Lily's inquiries lead to confrontations with Amaya security chief Kenton (Zach Grenier) and lead engineer Katie (Alison Pill), and eventually unravels Lily's grip on reality. Concepts spun off the idea that quantum computing, an evolutionary step beyond binary computing, allow developers to mathematically reveal multiplicities of past or future events. "There were a lot of 'what-if's," noted Garland, "but the story took a scientific principle and ran with it. The idea was that we have binary computers, but we exist 2 / 22 in a quantum mechanical world. When you use a binary computer to model a quantum

As you certainly know, the industry we cover has been particularly hard-hit by the coronavirus pandemic, with worldwide theater closuresand an entire season of major effects releases pushed back to later in the year or even into next. As of this writing, it remains uncertain when theaters will reopen and whether films still slated for release this summer will indeed be launched as scheduled. Cinefex article require weeks, even months of research and writing. Without approval from the major film studios, the effects companies and artists behind these upcoming releases are forbidden to discuss their work on these projects, and that approval is being withheld amidst the current uncertainty. So, with three issues published thus far this year, we are at a virtual standstill, and have decided our best course of action is go on hiatus for the next few months, and resume publication in December, when we can catch up on the films released between now and then. We look forward to rejoining you at that time, and returning to our bimonthly schedule in 2021. As subscribers, rest assured, your subscription term will be automatically extended, and you will receive all of the issues to which you are entitled. See you in December. Team Cinefex
